content: The follicular phase, also known as the proliferative phase, is a stage of the menstrual cycle (or the estrous cycle in non-human mammals) during which ovarian follicles mature. This phase concludes with ovulation, and its primary regulatory hormone is estradiol. Hormonal Events Follicle Recruitment Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. FSH levels begin to rise during the final days of the previous menstrual cycle and peak during the first week of the follicular phase. This increase in FSH recruits five to seven tertiary-stage ovarian follicles (also referred to as Graafian or antral follicles) to enter the menstrual cycle. These follicles, which have been developing for nearly a year through a process called folliculogenesis, compete for dominance. FSH stimulates the proliferation of granulosa cells within the developing follicles and promotes the expression of luteinizing hormone (LH) receptors on these granulosa cells. Under the influence of FSH, aromatase and P450 enzymes are activated, leading to the secretion of estrogen by granulosa cells. The rising estrogen levels stimulate the production of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), which in turn increases LH production. LH promotes androgen synthesis by thecal cells, stimulates the proliferation and differentiation of follicular thecal cells, and enhances LH receptor expression on granulosa cells. Estrogen Surge Two to three days after LH levels begin to rise, one (or occasionally two) of the recruited follicles becomes dominant. Many endocrinologists believe that the dominant follicle's estrogen secretion increases to a level that suppresses GnRH production, thereby reducing LH and FSH levels. This suppression leads to the atresia (degeneration) of most of the recruited follicles, while the dominant follicle continues to mature. Estrogen levels continue to rise for several days (on average, six days, though this duration varies). Elevated estrogen levels stimulate the formation of a new layer of endometrium in the uterus, histologically identified as proliferative endometrium. Cervical crypts are also stimulated to produce fertile cervical mucus, which reduces vaginal acidity and creates a more favorable environment for sperm. This mucus has a specific texture that facilitates sperm movement through the cervix and into the fallopian tubes, where they await ovulation. Additionally, basal body temperature may slightly decrease under the influence of high estrogen levels. LH Surge and Ovulation Estrogen levels reach their peak just before the LH surge begins. A temporary drop in steroid hormone levels between the onset of the LH surge and ovulation may cause mid-cycle spotting or bleeding. The preovulatory LH surge triggers the first meiotic division in oocytes and initiates luteinization of thecal and granulosa cells. Ovulation typically occurs approximately 30 hours (±2 hours) after the onset of the LH surge, which is when LH first becomes detectable in urine. Follicular Waves The time from the recruitment of tertiary-stage follicles to ovulation is generally about two weeks, corresponding to days 1–14 of an idealized 28-day menstrual cycle. However, the follicular phase can last significantly longer if no dominant follicle is selected. In such cases, additional tertiary-stage follicles are recruited, and the process begins again. A study of women with regular menstrual cycles found that none ovulated after the first wave of follicle development. Instead, 68% of cycles showed ovulation after the second wave, while 32% showed ovulation after the third wave. Fertility awareness sources may refer to these multiple waves of follicular development as a split peak due to the characteristic pattern of cervical mucus changes that can sometimes be observed.
